Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette: Elias Vance had spent twelve years reading the quiet rhythms of the Pacific Northwest as a park ranger, until a six-day captivity stripped him of that certainty. His captors had kept him blindfolded in a windowless room, controlled his access to food and water, and deliberately manipulated time so that every long silence felt like a precursor to worse violence. The interrogator would leave him alone for hours, then return with new injuries already prepared, teaching Elias that pauses in the room’s routine always preceded pain. Now, the trauma refused to settle into a coherent narrative. When he tries to explain what happened he loses the thread and cannot finish, and some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank. The nonverbal memory of cold concrete and sharp pain would surface without words, which only deepened his conviction that his body has been permanently damaged by what happened. Because he could not piece the experience together, he began to believe he could not rely on other people to keep him safe. Over the following months, his belief that he could not rely on other people directly shaped how he scanned his environment. Since he feared he would be left defenseless, when something takes longer than expected he assumes something bad is happening. This dread made him treat ordinary pauses as impending threats, which meant his body reacts before mind whenever a door clicked or an engine idled. The constant vigilance fractured his recall further, meaning he could not explain clearly because the sensory overload scattered his thoughts. To cope with the escalating anxiety, he rehearse what to say before any interaction, running through every possible question in advance so he would never lose control. But this mental rehearsal blocked his ability to process the event, which made his partial clarity feel even more fragmented, and the resulting emotional numbing convinced him that he is going crazy. The numbing left him detached from his own warnings, which only amplified his threat monitoring. He started to check doors and lock checking every window repeatedly, a frantic attempt to force the world into a predictable shape. The exhaustion of these checks drained his hope that anyone could help him, which reinforced his belief he cannot rely on others, which in turn made the fractured recall feel even more unbearable. When the partial clarity of the trauma surfaced, his body reacts before mind as if the danger is still present. To protect himself from those sudden physiological alerts, he avoid driving to keep himself near the ranger station where he could control his exit routes. This avoidance cut him off from his colleagues, which cemented his fear that he is going crazy. Yet his inability to form a clear account only proved to him that his body has been permanently damaged, which meant he could not rely on other people, leaving him isolated in a loop of his own making. The constant dread of delays only tightened his focus on potential traps, which meant he could not explain clearly, and the resulting paralysis made him rehearse conversations with even more desperate intensity. At the station, the weight of his patrol gear now felt like restraint, and the silence of the forest floor mirrored the concrete room he had escaped but never left. What finally brought him to seek help was a breakdown during a routine patrol when he froze, unable to drive toward a reported wildfire because his body reacted before mind and his mind refused to explain clearly. He is terrified that his emotions will remain buried under numbing if he cannot process the event, but he is hoping a therapist might help him untangle the rehearsal habits and finally trust that the past is over.
